newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Slow productivity gains frustrate Anglo.
newsitem.headline: Slow productivity gains frustrate Anglo.

text.p: Despite good second quarter gold results Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd's gold division, Anglogold, said on Thursday it was frustrated by the slow progress being made in improving labour productivity.
Speaking at the presentation of the group's second quarter results, Anglogold chief executive Bobby Godsell said:

"Whilst the quarter presents good financial and reasonable operational results, the fundamental breakthrough in operational efficiencies and labour productivity is proving frustratingly slow. It is disappointing at how long it is taking."
Anglogold announced that available profits from its gold mines in the three months to end-June fell to 220.7 million rand ($48.4 million), down two percent on the previous March quarter.
Godsell said that although progress was being made towards the labour efficiency targets set at the beginning of the year, the change in mindset was far from achieved.
"Against this background, this year's industry wage and productivity agreement is an important step forward," he said.

Earlier this month the National Union of Mineworkers and the Chamber of Mines employer representative body signed an interim industry agreement to raise overall production by 90 tonnes this year in return for a two-year wage deal which could see wages rise between nine and 25 percent.

Godsell said Anglogold needs 10.5 additional tonnes of profitable gold this year to pay for wage increases and would not pay increases until it was confident the extra profitable production would be achieved.

"For the Anglogold comapnies we are utterly determined not to increase unit costs of production. In the present price scenario we would be suicidal to do this. Therefore, the incremental cost of the wage increase at least must be fully met by improved revenue generation," Godsell said.
But he added that "cost neutrality" was not enough.

"Our goal of reducing cash operating costs to below the $250 per ounce level remains, and only the fundamental restructuring of almost all aspects of present mining practice can achieve this," Godsell said.
He said the new productivity-linked wage deal sought to change the nature of union/management wage bargaining.

"Wage bargaining has been arm wrestling accompanied by marches and pickets and go-slows to get a higher percentage wage increase. We're trying to change the agenda into a developmental agenda," Godsell said.

Steve Lenahan, Anglogold's executive director for industrial relations, said progress on the productivity wage deal was mixed but encouraging with two of the four shafts on the West Rand moving towards an arrangement providing for an additional 19 shifts per year.
Freegold was moving towards extending its operating calendar, workplace restructuring and employee re-training.
But some employees at Vaal Reefs' key long-life shafts -- Nos 8,9 and 10 -- were resisting the implementation of a new longer working calendar
